title: Bosonic Error Correction with Fluxonium
authors: Shantanu R. Jha, Shoumik D. Chowdhury, Gabriele Rolleri, Anaida Ali, Lev-Arcady Sellem, Réouven Assouly, David Pahl, Lukas Pahl, Junyoung An, Farid Hassani, Hung-Yu Tsao, Chia-Chin Tsai, Aranya Goswami, Jeremie Boudreault, Jeffrey M. Gertler, Michael A. Gingras, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Jeffrey M. Knecht, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Jeffrey A. Grover, Baptiste Royer, Max Hays, William D. Oliver
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) offers a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing. To date, however, superconducting circuit implementations of bosonic codes have utilized centimeter-scale 3D microwave cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmon qubits, with logical lifetimes limited by transmon bit-flip errors. Here, we realize bosonic QEC in a fully planar architecture by pairing a heavy fluxonium, whose $451 \pm 70~μ\mathrm{s}$ bit-flip lifetime exceeds that of any control qubit in previous demonstrations, with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator several orders of magnitude smaller in mode volume than prior 3D cavities. We prepare finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilize them using measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending the logical lifetime by a factor of $1.59 \pm 0.05$. These results provide the first demonstration of resonator control using a weakly coupled fluxonium and, with it, the first realization of standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture.
summary: This paper reports the first realization of bosonic quantum error correction in a fully planar superconducting circuit. By coupling a long-lived fluxonium qubit to a small, planar resonator, the authors successfully prepared GKP logical states and demonstrated error correction, extending the logical coherence time by a factor of 1.59.
main_problem: The primary goal is to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computation using bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) in a scalable hardware platform.
main_result: The authors demonstrated the first standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture, achieving a logical lifetime enhancement factor of $1.59 \pm 0.05$.
method: The technique involves preparing finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilizing them using measurement-free error correction implemented via rapid fluxonium reset.
model_or_system: The system uses a heavy fluxonium qubit coupled dispersively to an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator (ASR). The control relies on the weak coupling regime and the fluxonium's long bit-flip lifetime.
key_observables: Logical lifetimes ($T_C$), fluxonium excited-state population $P(e)$ vs. photon number ($ ar{n}$), and Husimi Q-functions of the resonator state.
important_parameters: Fluxonium bit-flip lifetime ($451 \pm 70 \mu s$), resonator quality factor ($Q = 2.65 	imes 10^6$), and the logical lifetime enhancement factor ($1.59 \pm 0.05$).
main_assumptions: The fluxonium is operated at the half-flux sweet spot ($\Phi_{	ext{ext}} = \Phi_0/2$) to minimize flux noise sensitivity, and the weak coupling regime is maintained.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the error correction protocol mapping errors from the resonator to the fluxonium followed by reset. Figure 2 shows characterization of the ECD gate action via Q-functions and characteristic functions of cat states.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup (fluxonium coupled to ASR), the implementation of necessary quantum control gates (ECD), the preparation of GKP states, and finally, the measurement and demonstration of the measurement-free error correction protocol.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware limitations of superconducting QEC by moving to a planar architecture and utilizing a high-coherence qubit (fluxonium) for error syndrome extraction.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Fluxonium-resonator device. (a) Schematic of the fluxonium-resonator system, with the flow of liquid rep- resenting errors entering and leaving the system. The error- correction protocol maps errors from the resonator (green) to the fluxonium (purple) at a controllable rate, represented by the middle tunable valve. The fluxonium is then reset at a controllable rate, represented by the leftmost valve, removing the errors from the system. Error correction thus acts as engi- neered dissipation that restores the system to the code space. (b) False-colored optical micrograph of the device, with the fluxonium and its flux line in purple, ASR in green, readout resonator stub in dark grey,...
